mac_awake.mac_reference_basis: each patient's own age-adjusted MAC (Katoh 1993, slow washout, descending)

sources.citation: De Wolf AM, Van Zundert TC, De Cooman S, Hendrickx JF. Theoretical effect of hyperventilation on speed of recovery and risk of rehypnotization following recovery - a Gas Man simulation. BMC Anesthesiology. 2012;12:22.
sources.note: Tier 3, reference implementation (see docs/MODEL.md, 'Source hierarchy'). Table 1 reports the Gas Man isoflurane blood:gas and tissue:gas coefficients used here, in the same table already cited for sevoflurane. De Wolf et al. ran Gas Man simulations and measured no coefficient: Table 1 is the parameter set they supplied to it, so this is the Gas Man set carrying a journal's name rather than a measurement. It is the source of the stored values.

sources.citation: Yasuda N, Targ AG, Eger EI II. Solubility of I-653, sevoflurane, isoflurane, and halothane in human tissues. Anesthesia & Analgesia. 1989;69(3):370-373.
sources.note: Tier 1, primary measurement, cited but not adopted. Human tissue study reporting an isoflurane brain:blood partition coefficient of 1.57 +/- 0.10 at 37 degrees C. The stored tissue:gas values are Gas Man's; dividing vessel_rich by blood:gas gives an implied brain:blood of 2.1/1.3 = 1.615, 2.9 percent above Yasuda's measurement and the loosest of the three agents. Same paper already cited for sevoflurane's and desflurane's tissue-solubility models, where the group-weighting obstacle to adopting it is recorded.

sources.citation: Malviya S, Lerman J. The blood/gas solubilities of sevoflurane, isoflurane, halothane, and serum constituent concentrations in neonates and adults. Anesthesiology. 1990;72(5):793-796.
sources.note: Tier 1, primary measurement, cited but not adopted, and not the source of the adult number: it confirms that isoflurane's blood:gas coefficient was measured directly in adult humans and differs from neonates, but its abstract does not carry the adult value. Lerman et al. 1984 below is the paper that does.

sources.citation: Lerman J, Gregory GA, Willis MM, Eger EI II. Age and solubility of volatile anesthetics in blood. Anesthesiology. 1984;61(2):139-143.
sources.note: Tier 1, primary measurement, cited but not adopted. Blood:gas partition coefficients measured in fasting subjects by age group: isoflurane 1.46 in adults aged 20-40 (n=11), 1.29 in the elderly aged 75-85, 1.28 in children aged 3-7, 1.19 in full-term newborns. The adult 1.46 is the measurement the textbook's rounded 1.4 rests on. The stored value 1.3 is the Gas Man figure and is 11.0 percent lower than 1.46 - the widest gap between a stored value and its primary measurement in this project. PL-D6LX carries the decision for all three agents; PL-T531 carries the 1.3-versus-1.4 question folded into it.

sources.citation: Kelly JM, Kong K-L. Accuracy of ten isoflurane vaporisers in current clinical use. Anaesthesia. 2011;66(8):682-688.
sources.note: Primary source for a device capability: docs/MODEL.md's source hierarchy concerns measured physiologic quantities, and a calibrated dial maximum is not one. Studies the two standard isoflurane vaporizers in current clinical use (Penlon Sigma Delta, Datex-Ohmeda Isotec 5), both calibrated 0-5%. Used here as max_delivered_concentration_percent. This is a device-capability limit on the delivered-concentration control, not a scientific model parameter; it does not affect the governing equations.

sources.citation: Nickalls RWD, Mapleson WW. Age-related iso-MAC charts for isoflurane, sevoflurane and desflurane in man. British Journal of Anaesthesia. 2003;91(2):170-174.
sources.note: The stored mac_percent is tier 3: it is the flat adult MAC De Wolf et al. state they used in their Gas Man simulations, not a value taken from this paper. Nickalls and Mapleson is cited but not adopted. It is tier 2, not tier 1 - its own abstract states the charts "are based on Mapleson's meta-analysis (1996) of the available MAC data", so it synthesises measurements rather than making one, and docs/MODEL.md's source hierarchy does not admit tier 2 as the authority for a stored value. It is also age-related, and this project's reference-adult model has no age parameter, so mac_percent uses the flat adult value from De Wolf et al. above (same paper already cited for partition coefficients: 'MAC values that we used in our Gas Man simulations are: desflurane 6%, sevoflurane 2%, isoflurane 1.2%'). Used as the controller's starting delivered-concentration default (1 MAC) and as the divisor of the interface's MAC-multiple display unit; it is not a governing-equation parameter and no equation in core/ reads it. See docs/MODEL.md, 'MAC multiples as a display unit' and 'Delivery-limit and MAC parameters'.

sources.citation: Mapleson WW. Effect of age on MAC in humans: a meta-analysis. British Journal of Anaesthesia. 1996;76(2):179-185.
sources.note: Tier 2, secondary synthesis, cited but not adopted; the source of the age-40 MAC this project's stored value is measured against. Regression of a comprehensive literature survey, reporting MAC at age 40 as 1.17 percent for isoflurane (95% confidence limits about plus or minus 7 percent for isoflurane and sevoflurane and 10 percent for desflurane), and MAC falling about 6 percent per decade of age. The stored mac_percent of 1.2 percent is 2.6 percent higher. Not adopted for two reasons: a meta-analysis measures nothing and is tier 2 under docs/MODEL.md's source hierarchy, which admits only tier 1 as the authority for a stored value; and every other parameter in this model is the Gas Man set, so a Mapleson divisor over a Gas Man trajectory would make each displayed MAC multiple a ratio between two parameter lineages. The consequence is displayed and disclosed rather than silently absorbed: against this source the interface's MAC multiples for isoflurane read 2.5 percent low, and because the sevoflurane and desflurane errors run in opposite directions a cross-agent comparison at '1 MAC' is displaced by about 22 percent. docs/MODEL.md, 'Known limitations', carries that; ROADMAP.md's planned-milestone item 31 is the route to primary values.

sources.citation: Katoh T, Suguro Y, Kimura T, Ikeda K. Cerebral awakening concentration of sevoflurane and isoflurane predicted during slow and fast alveolar washout. Anesthesia & Analgesia. 1993;77(5):1012-1017.
sources.note: Tier 1, primary measurement, and the source of the stored mac_awake. 49 ASA I patients; MAC-awake was determined as the average of the bracketing alveolar concentrations that allow and prevent response to verbal command during recovery, and reported "as a ratio to age-adjusted MAC". That ratio is what is stored: it is the form the paper reports, and the only form that stays correct if mac_percent is ever changed or made age-aware. Slow washout (concentration decreased in 15-minute steps, brain assumed equilibrated with alveolar gas) gave 0.31 +/- 0.05 for isoflurane; fast washout (discontinuation from 0.5 MAC) gave 0.22 +/- 0.05 MAC, significantly smaller, and the paper attributes the difference to end-tidal-to-arterial and arterial-to-cerebral anesthetic differences - which is what this model represents as the alveolar-to-vessel-rich difference. The slow-washout figure is the one stored because it is the *brain* concentration at awakening, and the paper measures that directly rather than leaving it to inference: cerebral concentration at first eye opening during fast washout was 0.30 +/- 0.08 MAC, "nearly equal to MAC-Awake obtained by slow alveolar washout". That is why docs/MODEL.md requires the band to be read against the vessel-rich trace. Determination is descending (during washout); the desflurane value in desflurane.json is ascending, and the two are not interchangeable methods. Retrieved from PubMed (PMID 8214700) and verified against the abstract 2026-09-04.
